propositions.text: Mr. Chung was acquitted of dangerous driving causing death under s. 249(4) of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: Mr. Chung was acquitted of dangerous driving causing death under s. 249(4) [1] of the Criminal Code , R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 (“Code ”).

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Chung drove dangerously but had reasonable doubt about mens rea.
propositions.quote: the trial judge had a reasonable doubt about whether Mr. Chung had the requisite guilty mind or mens rea (2018 BCPC 133, 29 M.V.R. (7th) 122).

propositions.text: On appeal, sole issue was whether trial judge erred in law in finding lack of mens rea.
propositions.quote: On appeal, the sole issue was whether the trial judge committed an error of law in finding that Mr. Chung lacked the requisite mens rea (2019 BCCA 206, 55 C.R. (7th) 459).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found trial judge erred in law and overturned acquittal.
propositions.quote: The British Columbia Court of Appeal found such an error of law.

propositions.text: This Court concludes there was an error of law and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Reading the trial judgment fully and fairly, I conclude that there was an error of law and that this appeal must be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Mr. Chung was acquitted but trial judge had doubt on mens rea; Court of Appeal found legal error; this Court dismisses appeal for error of law.

propositions.text: On Nov 14, 2015, Mr. Chung drove nearly three times the speed limit and crashed into a left-turning vehicle, killing its driver.
propositions.quote: On the morning of Saturday, November 14, 2015, Mr. Chung drove his vehicle at almost three times the speed limit towards a major intersection in Vancouver and crashed into a left-turning vehicle. The driver of the left-turning vehicle died at the scene.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Mr. Chung drove nearly three times the speed limit and caused a fatal crash on Nov 14, 2015.

propositions.text: Collision occurred at Oak Street and West 41st Avenue, a mixed residential-commercial area with pedestrians and witnesses present.
propositions.quote: The collision occurred at the intersection of two arterial roads in Vancouver: Oak Street and West 41st Avenue. This was a mixed residential-commercial area with two gas stations, a community centre, a nursing home, small retail businesses, and multiple bus stops around and near the intersection. Four pedestrians were in the vicinity of the intersection at the time of the collision. It was not raining, but the road was damp or wet. Traffic was light around the intersection, but other cars were present and five civilian witnesses were called at trial who were all driving cars near the intersection at the time of the collision. The speed limit for both streets is 50 km/h, but drivers generally go above that speed limit. Both roads are wide and straight and have dedicated left turning lanes.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the collision location, environment, witnesses, weather, traffic, and speed limits.

propositions.text: Dashboard camera video showed Mr. Chung accelerated from 50 to 140 km/h, passed cars, and collided at 119 km/h after braking.
propositions.quote: A dashboard camera video from another vehicle at the intersection captured 4.9 seconds of the event. Over the span of a block, Mr. Chung had moved into the curbside lane, passed at least one car on the right, and accelerated from 50 km/h to 140 km/h before entering the intersection. The trial judge found that Mr. Chung was not inattentive nor was he engaged in any dangerous conduct prior to this one block span. Mr. Chung was driving a powerful vehicle that could accelerate quickly; the trial judge heard expert evidence that the vehicle could accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 4.5 seconds in dry conditions, although the trial judge made no findings regarding exactly how quickly Mr. Chung reached his top speed in damp or wet conditions. As Mr. Chung approached the intersection going north along Oak Street, there was a Toyota in front of him making a right turn. As the Toyota was turning right, the victim started to make his left turn from going southbound on Oak Street to eastbound on West 41st Avenue. At this point, Mr. Chung started braking, narrowly missed hitting the Toyota, and collided with the victim’s car at a speed of 119 km/h.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states video showed Mr. Chung accelerated rapidly, passed cars, braked, narrowly missed a Toyota, then collided at 119 km/h.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Chung’s speeding over a short distance was objectively dangerous and established actus reus of dangerous driving.
propositions.quote: Taking into account all of the above circumstances, the trial judge found that Mr. Chung’s excessive speeding over a short distance towards this major intersection was objectively dangerous to the public and that the actus reus of dangerous driving was established.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Mr. Chung’s short-distance excessive speeding objectively dangerous and established actus reus.

propositions.text: Trial judge acquitted Mr. Chung due to reasonable doubt about mens rea, emphasizing momentariness of speeding.
propositions.quote: However, the trial judge acquitted Mr. Chung because he had reasonable doubt that Mr. Chung’s conduct met the mens rea requirement for dangerous driving. The trial judge distinguished the facts of this case from circumstances where excessive speed met the mens rea requirement and emphasized that the momentariness of Mr. Chung’s speeding was critical in finding that his conduct did not show criminal fault.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge acquitted Mr. Chung due to reasonable doubt on mens rea, focusing on momentariness of speeding.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found trial judge erred in law by wrongly applying principle that brief speeding cannot satisfy mens rea.
propositions.quote: The British Columbia Court of Appeal found that the trial judge had erred in law by “conceiv[ing] that a principle exists that a brief period of speeding (no matter how excessive the speed) cannot satisfy the mens rea requirement” (para. 42).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal overturned acquittal and entered conviction due to trial judge’s error.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal therefore overturned the acquittal and entered a conviction, ruling that Mr. Chung would have been found guilty but for the trial judge’s error.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found trial judge erred by applying a principle that brief speeding cannot satisfy mens rea and overturned acquittal.

propositions.text: Sole issue is whether trial judge erred in law, allowing Crown to appeal acquittal under s. 676(1)(a) of the Code.
propositions.quote: The sole issue in this appeal is whether the trial judge made an error of law, which would allow the Crown to appeal Mr. Chung’s acquittal under s. 676(1) (a) of the Code .

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the sole issue is whether the trial judge erred in law, permitting Crown appeal under s. 676(1)(a).

propositions.text: The reasons will first describe reviewable errors, then interpret trial judge’s reasons showing errors, then explain dismissal of appeal.
propositions.quote: In these reasons, I first describe the types of errors that are reviewable by appellate courts for Crown appeals of acquittals. Second, I interpret the trial judge’s reasons and explain how they demonstrate two inter-related errors of law concerning the interpretation and application of the test for mens rea for dangerous driving. Lastly, I address why I would dismiss the appeal and uphold the conviction entered by the Court of Appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court outlines its reasons: reviewable errors, trial judge’s errors, and dismissal of appeal.

propositions.text: Under s. 676(1)(a), Crown can only appeal acquittal on question of law alone, not on unreasonable acquittal.
propositions.quote: Under s. 676(1)(a), the Crown can only appeal an acquittal on a “question of law alone”. An appealable error must be traced to a question of law, rather than a question about how to weigh evidence and assess whether it meets the standard of proof (R. v. J.M.H., 2011 SCC 45, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 197, at paras. 25-27; R. v. George, 2017 SCC 38, [2017] 1 S.C.R. 1021, at paras. 15-17). Therefore, the Crown cannot appeal merely because an acquittal is unreasonable (R. v. Biniaris, 2000 SCC 15, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 381, at para. 33).

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Crown appeals under s. 676(1)(a) are limited to questions of law, not unreasonable acquittals.

propositions.text: Errors of law include legal effect of facts raising legal question or evidence assessed on wrong legal principle.
propositions.quote: Errors of law arise, for example, where “the legal effect of findings of fact or of undisputed facts raises a question of law” and where there is “an assessment of the evidence based on a wrong legal principle” (J.M.H., at paras. 28-30).

propositions.text: These errors show trial judge’s erroneous understanding of law in applying legal principles to evidence.
propositions.quote: These two types of errors are somewhat similar; they both address errors where the trial judge’s application of the legal principles to the evidence demonstrates an erroneous understanding of the law, either because the trial judge finds all the facts necessary to meet the test but errs in law in its application, or assesses the evidence in a way that otherwise indicates a misapprehension of the law.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains errors of law include legal effect of facts raising legal questions or wrong legal principle application.

propositions.text: Mr. Chung argues there is no error of law in trial judge’s reasons.
propositions.quote: Mr. Chung argues that there is no such error of law in the trial judge’s reasons.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Mr. Chung that there is no error of law.
propositions.quote: I disagree.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Chung argues no error of law; the Court disagrees.

propositions.text: Appellate courts should read trial judge’s reasons as a whole, not line-by-line, considering context and purpose.
propositions.quote: When interpreting a trial judge’s reasons, appellate courts should not parse the reasons of the trial judge in a line by line search for errors. Instead, the reasons are to be “read as a whole, in the context of the evidence, the issues and the arguments at trial, together with ‘an appreciation of the purposes or functions for which they are delivered’” (R. v. Laboucan, 2010 SCC 12, [2010] 1 S.C.R. 397, at para. 16, quoting R. v. R.E.M., 2008 SCC 51, [2008] 3 S.C.R. 3, at para. 16).

propositions.text: Even if trial judge states correct test, appellate court may find error if reasoning shows failure to properly apprehend law.
propositions.quote: Appellate courts must attempt to understand the reasoning of the trial judge. However, even if the trial judge articulates the right test, appellate courts may find an error of law if the judge’s reasoning and application demonstrate a failure to properly apprehend the law (George, at para. 16).

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains appellate courts read trial reasons as a whole and may find legal error despite correct test articulation.

propositions.text: Trial judge reviewed evidence and cited correct test for mens rea from R. v. Roy.
propositions.quote: In this case, the trial judge thoroughly reviewed the evidence before him and made clear factual findings. He cited, at para. 63, the correct test for the mens rea of dangerous driving causing death, articulated in R. v. Roy, 2012 SCC 26, [2012] 2 S.C.R. 60, at para. 36: The focus of the mens rea analysis is on whether the dangerous manner of driving was the result of a marked departure from the standard of care which a reasonable person would have exercised in the same circumstances (Beatty, at para. 48).

propositions.text: The mens rea test involves whether a reasonable person would have foreseen risk and taken steps to avoid it, and whether failure to do so was a marked departure.
propositions.quote: It is helpful to approach the issue by asking two questions. The first is whether, in light of all the relevant evidence, a reasonable person would have foreseen the risk and taken steps to avoid it if possible. If so, the second question is whether the accused’s failure to foresee the risk and take steps to avoid it, if possible, was a marked departure from the standard of care expected of a reasonable person in the accused’s circumstances. [Emphasis in original.]

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge reviewed evidence and cited correct mens rea test from R. v. Roy involving reasonable person’s foresight and marked departure.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Chung’s dangerous conduct limited to one block of acceleration and collision, and not inattentive.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that Mr. Chung’s dangerous conduct was only limited to the one block span where he accelerated to almost three times the speed limit, passing at least one car on the right, nearly hit the Toyota turning right in front of him, and then collided with the victim’s vehicle. The trial judge concluded that Mr. Chung had not been inattentive while driving.

propositions.text: Trial judge believed speeding alone rarely establishes mens rea unless more than momentary or with other dangerous conduct.
propositions.quote: The trial judge then canvassed a line of cases which he believed supported the principle that speeding alone is rarely sufficient to establish the mens rea for dangerous driving. He distinguished these cases, finding that in these cases speeding was more than momentary or there was some other additional dangerous conduct that was not present in the case at bar.

propositions.text: Trial judge emphasized momentariness of speeding as critical, leading to reasonable doubt on marked departure.
propositions.quote: The trial judge emphasized that Mr. Chung’s speed was momentary, noting that although momentary conduct can be a marked departure, it will more usually be only a mere departure where driving is otherwise proper (para. 117, citing R. v. Willock (2006), 212 O.A.C. 82, per Doherty J.A.). Therefore, he had reasonable doubt that Mr. Chung’s conduct represented a marked departure because the “momentariness of the accused’s conduct in excessively speeding [was] insufficient to meet the criminal fault component” (paras. 119-120).

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Mr. Chung’s dangerous conduct limited to one block, believed speeding alone rarely shows mens rea unless more than momentary, and emphasized momentariness causing reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: It is error of law if trial judge fails to compare accused’s actions to reasonable person’s foresight and conduct in all circumstances.
propositions.quote: However, it would be an error of law if the trial judge failed to compare the accused’s actions to what a reasonable person would have foreseen and done in all of the circumstances. This type of error is not a factual matter of weighing evidence, but rather it goes to the legal definition of the mens rea analysis for dangerous driving.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states failure to compare accused’s actions to reasonable person’s foresight is an error of law, not a factual issue.

propositions.text: Court finds two inter-related errors of law: applying wrong legal principle and failing to apply correct legal test from Roy.
propositions.quote: Although the trial judge correctly cited passages from cases which express the applicable legal standards, I find two inter-related errors of law. First, I agree with the Court of Appeal that the trial judge erred by applying a wrong legal principle. Second, and most importantly, I find that the trial judge failed to apply the correct legal test in Roy by not assessing what a reasonable person would have foreseen and done in Mr. Chung’s circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds trial judge erred by applying wrong legal principle and failing to apply correct legal test from Roy.

propositions.text: Applying wrong legal principle and failing to apply correct test are two sides of same error: failure to consider reasonable person’s conduct in all circumstances.
propositions.quote: Applying a wrong legal principle and failing to apply the correct legal test are two sides of the same coin. Both characterizations go to the same essential error of law in this case, which was a failure of the trial judge to properly consider the conduct of the reasonable person in all of the circumstances in determining whether there was a marked departure.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains both errors reflect failure to consider reasonable person’s conduct in all circumstances for marked departure.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Court of Appeal that trial judge’s focus on momentariness of speeding is legal error.
propositions.quote: First, I agree with the Court of Appeal that the trial judge’s fixation on the momentariness of the speeding demonstrates an error of law.

propositions.text: Momentary excessive speeding can establish mens rea if it supports inference of marked departure from reasonable person’s standard of care.
propositions.quote: Clearly, momentary excessive speeding on its own can establish the mens rea for dangerous driving where, having regard to all the circumstances, it supports an inference that the driving was the result of a marked departure from the standard of care that a reasonable person in the same circumstances would have exhibited (Roy, at para. 41).

paragraphs.summary: The Court agrees with Court of Appeal that focusing on momentariness is error; momentary speeding can establish mens rea if it shows marked departure.

propositions.text: Trial judge relied on legal principle that momentary excessive speed alone cannot establish mens rea, citing Willock and distinguishing other cases.
propositions.quote: Although the trial judge recognized that momentary conduct could be a marked departure, the trial judge stated that his analysis turned “[c]ritically” on the fact that Mr. Chung’s speed was categorically momentary (para. 117). That the trial judge was relying on a legal principle, rather than making a determination of fact, is supported by his citation to Willock and the fact that he distinguished other cases where excessive speeding and acceleration occurred over a longer period of time or in conjunction with additional dangerous conduct (paras. 103-7 and 118). Read as a whole, his reasons indicate that he believed that, when excessive speed was momentary, it was unable on its own to establish the mens rea for dangerous driving.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds trial judge relied on legal principle that momentary excessive speed alone cannot establish mens rea, citing Willock and distinguishing cases.

propositions.text: The trial judge erred by focusing on momentary nature of conduct instead of whether reasonable person would foresee dangers from momentary conduct.
propositions.quote: The trial judge erred in focussing on the momentary nature of Mr. Chung’s conduct, rather than analyzing whether the reasonable person would foresee the dangers to the public from the momentary conduct.

propositions.text: Brief rapid lane changes and acceleration are not comparable to momentary mistakes like mistimed turns or momentary loss of awareness.
propositions.quote: A brief period of rapidly changing lanes and accelerating towards an intersection is not comparable to momentary mistakes that may be made by any reasonable driver, like the mistimed turn on to a highway in Roy, the momentary loss of awareness in R. v. Beatty, 2008 SCC 5, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 49, or the sudden loss of control in Willock.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge erred by focusing on momentary conduct rather than foreseeability of danger, and that brief rapid lane changes differ from momentary mistakes.

propositions.text: Momentary lapses usually do not raise criminal liability because they result from automatic reflexive driving or simple carelessness.
propositions.quote: momentary lapses often result from the “automatic and reflexive nature of driving” (Beatty, at para. 34) or “[s]imple carelessness, to which even the most prudent drivers may occasionally succumb” (Roy, at para. 37).

propositions.text: Momentary conduct is assessed like other dangerous conduct; brief conduct creating foreseeable immediate risks can be a marked departure.
propositions.quote: Momentary conduct is not assessed differently from other dangerous conduct. Conduct that occurs over a brief period of time that creates foreseeable and immediate risks of serious consequences can still be a marked departure from the norm (Beatty, at para. 48).

propositions.text: A reasonable person would foresee that rapidly accelerating towards a major intersection at high speed creates a real collision risk.
propositions.quote: A reasonable person would have foreseen that rapidly accelerating towards a major intersection at a high speed creates a very real risk of a collision occurring within seconds.

propositions.text: Foreseeable immediate consequences from momentary dangerous conduct do not preclude finding mens rea for dangerous driving.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the fact that foreseeable consequences occur within a short period of time after someone engages in highly dangerous behaviour cannot preclude a finding of mens rea for dangerous driving.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains momentary lapses usually lack criminal liability but momentary dangerous conduct with foreseeable immediate risks can show mens rea.

propositions.text: The trial judge failed to apply the correct legal test from Roy regarding reasonable person foreseeability and marked departure.
propositions.quote: the trial judge did not apply the correct legal test in Roy. In his reasons, he failed to determine whether a reasonable person in Mr. Chung’s circumstances would have foreseen the risk from accelerating rapidly and speeding into that major intersection and taken actions to avoid it.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not address the core question of whether the dangerous driving was a marked departure from reasonable care.
propositions.quote: he failed to undertake this analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge failed to apply Roy's legal test and did not analyze whether the conduct was a marked departure from reasonable care.

propositions.text: Trial judges need not write reasons in a particular way but Roy's two questions help compare accused's conduct to reasonable person standard.
propositions.quote: the two questions in Roy, at para. 36, are helpful and emphasize the need to compare the accused’s conduct to the conduct of a reasonable person in their circumstances

propositions.text: Determining objective mens rea requires considering all relevant evidence and whether reasonable person would foresee risk and act differently.
propositions.quote: At some point in the mens rea analysis, the trial judge must work with the facts as found and consider whether, in the totality of the circumstances, a reasonable person would have foreseen the risk and taken the same actions as the accused.

propositions.text: Only after full engagement with facts can trial judge decide if conduct was marked departure from reasonable driver.
propositions.quote: Only when there has been an active engagement with the full picture of what occurred can the trial judge determine whether the accused’s conduct was a marked departure from the conduct of a reasonable and prudent driver.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Roy's questions help trial judges compare conduct to reasonable person and fully engage facts to determine marked departure.

propositions.text: Trial judge wrongly focused on type and duration of conduct, excluding full picture and risks created by speeding.
propositions.quote: the trial judge engaged in reasoning focussed on the type (speeding) and duration (momentariness) of Mr. Chung’s conduct, to the exclusion of the full picture.

propositions.text: Trial judge compared what appellant did not do to other cases instead of assessing risks a reasonable person would foresee.
propositions.quote: he focussed on what Mr. Chung did not do in comparison to these other cases, rather than asking the correct legal question and assessing what risks a reasonable person would foresee arising from Mr. Chung’s momentary speeding in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge wrongly focused on conduct type and duration, ignoring full risk assessment and correct legal question.

propositions.text: Trial judge failed to consider full circumstances including lane changes, passing, acceleration, and awareness of other vehicles.
propositions.quote: Had the trial judge turned to consider the circumstances of this case fully and specifically, he would have addressed the fact that Mr. Chung’s conduct did not only include momentary excessive speeding, but also narrowly missing another vehicle turning right in front of him, passing in the curb lane, and accelerating towards a major intersection while aware of at least two vehicles in the intersection.

propositions.text: Trial judge found no inattentiveness but did not consider how awareness contributed to marked departure from reasonable conduct.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that Mr. Chung was not inattentive while driving, but did not consider how Mr. Chung’s awareness of his surroundings contributed to his conduct being a marked departure from the conduct of a reasonable person.

propositions.text: Full analysis requires considering duration, control, magnitude, location, and awareness to assess foreseeability and marked departure.
propositions.quote: A full analysis in this case would have considered the duration of the speeding, as well as the accused’s control of the car (he switched lanes and then accelerated), the magnitude of speeding (almost three times the speed limit), the location of speeding (approaching a major intersection), and the accused’s awareness of at least two vehicles at the intersection as he approached it.

propositions.text: Trial judge must consider if reasonable person would foresee risk and avoid it, presumably by not driving so fast.
propositions.quote: The trial judge then had to consider whether, on these facts as found, a reasonable person would have foreseen the risk of endangering the public by engaging in this conduct and taken steps to avoid it, presumably by not driving so fast.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge failed to consider full circumstances including awareness and control to assess foreseeability and marked departure.

propositions.text: Duration and nature of conduct are factors in mens rea analysis but must be considered in context with all circumstances.
propositions.quote: The duration and nature of the accused’s conduct are only some of the factors to be considered with all of the circumstances in the mens rea analysis.

propositions.text: Courts must avoid rigid rules about when isolated factors are marked departures and analyze conduct relative to reasonable person in specific circumstances.
propositions.quote: Courts must be careful to avoid fettering the analysis in Roy by adopting hard-and-fast rules regarding when isolated factors will or will not be marked departures.

propositions.text: Case law provides examples but courts must analyze accused’s actions relative to reasonable person in specific case.
propositions.quote: Although case law may be helpful in providing examples of what has previously been determined to be a marked departure, courts must still analyze the accused’s actions relative to the reasonable person in the specific circumstances at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court states duration and nature are factors but must be contextually analyzed; courts must avoid rigid rules and analyze relative to reasonable person.

propositions.text: Driving is inherently risky, more so with faster speed, harder acceleration, and aggressive navigation.
propositions.quote: A reasonable person understands that driving is an inherently risky activity. It is made all the more risky the faster we drive, the harder we accelerate, and the more aggressively we navigate traffic.

propositions.text: Some conduct is so dangerous it deserves criminal sanctions despite careful driving sometimes causing tragedy.
propositions.quote: some conduct is so dangerous that it deserves criminal sanctions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states driving is inherently risky and some conduct is so dangerous it deserves criminal sanctions.

propositions.text: Mr. Chung moved into curb lane, passed cars on right, accelerated to 140 km/h in 50 km/h zone near major intersection aware of other cars.
propositions.quote: Mr. Chung moved into the curb lane, passed at least one car on the right, and accelerated to 140 km/h in a 50 km/h zone while approaching a major urban intersection and being aware of at least two other cars in the intersection.

propositions.text: No evidence Mr. Chung lost control of vehicle.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence that the accused lost control of his vehicle.

propositions.text: Mens rea test is objective; subjective awareness or intent to create risk is not necessary.
propositions.quote: it is not necessary to find that Mr. Chung was subjectively aware of the risk of his conduct and intentionally created this risk. The test for mens rea is based on the reasonable person.

propositions.text: A reasonable person would foresee immediate risk of speeding nearly three times limit towards major intersection.
propositions.quote: A reasonable person would have foreseen the immediate risk of reaching a speed of almost three times the speed limit while accelerating towards a major city intersection.

propositions.text: Mr. Chung’s conduct is a marked departure from the norm.
propositions.quote: Mr. Chung’s conduct in these circumstances is a marked departure from the norm.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Chung’s high-speed conduct near intersection was a marked departure and a reasonable person would foresee immediate risk.

propositions.text: Trial judge made all necessary factual findings to support guilty verdict under s. 686(4)(b)(ii) of the Code.
propositions.quote: The trial judge made all the findings of fact necessary to determine that there was a marked departure from the standard of care of a reasonable and prudent driver, and therefore to support a verdict of guilty under s. 686(4) (b)(ii) of the Code

propositions.text: But for legal error, accused would have been convicted (R. v. Cassidy and R. v. Lutoslawski).
propositions.quote: In other words, but for the error of law, the accused would have been convicted (R. v. Cassidy, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 345, at p. 355). I would therefore dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge made necessary findings to support conviction but for legal error, so appeal is dismissed.

propositions.text: Crown appeals from acquittals are limited to questions of law under Criminal Code s. 676(1)(a).
propositions.quote: Crown rights of appeal from acquittals are limited to questions of law alone: Criminal Code , R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 676(1) (a).

propositions.text: No ground of unreasonable acquittal exists for Crown appeal; presumption of innocence and burden of proof prevent it (R. v. J.M.H., R. v. Biniaris).
propositions.quote: this Court has emphasized that there is no ground of “unreasonable acquittal” open to the Crown on appeal: see R. v. J.M.H., 2011 SCC 45, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 197, at paras. 32-33... the concept of ‘unreasonable acquittal’ is incompatible with the presumption of innocence and the burden which rests on the prosecution to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt

propositions.text: Appellate intervention only available if trial judge’s reasonable doubt is tainted by identifiable legal error (J.M.H.).
propositions.quote: Appellate intervention in an acquittal is only available when the Crown establishes that the trial judge’s reasonable doubt is tainted by an identifiable legal error: J.M.H., at para. 39.

propositions.text: Appellate jurisdiction does not extend to fact or mixed fact-law questions; Parliament limits Crown appeals from acquittals.
propositions.quote: Appellate jurisdiction does not extend to questions of fact and questions of mixed fact and law. Parliament’s clear policy choice to tightly circumscribe the scope of Crown appeals from acquittal must be respected.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Crown appeals from acquittals are limited to legal questions; no unreasonable acquittal ground exists; appellate intervention requires legal error.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s acquittal decision is not tainted by identifiable legal error.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the trial judge’s decision to acquit the appellant is not tainted by an identifiable legal error.

propositions.text: Appellant’s acquittal should be restored.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s acquittal should therefore be restored.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no legal error in trial judge’s acquittal and restores the acquittal.

propositions.text: Trial judges need not write perfect reasons; appellate courts read reasons as a whole, presuming knowledge of criminal law.
propositions.quote: Busy trial judges cannot be expected to write perfect reasons. Appellate courts approach a trial judge’s reasons by reading them as a whole rather than finely parsing them, presuming that the trial judge knows the basic principles of criminal law

propositions.text: Adequacy of trial judge’s reasons is informed by limited Crown appeal rights on acquittal; context calls for restraint.
propositions.quote: On a Crown appeal from an acquittal, this Court has further emphasized that the adequacy of a trial judge’s reasons is informed by the limited nature of the Crown’s appeal rights... This context calls for restraint

paragraphs.summary: The court states trial judges need not write perfect reasons; appellate courts read reasons as a whole and exercise restraint on Crown appeals.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found trial judge applied wrong legal standard, wrongly thinking brief speeding cannot satisfy mens rea.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge applied a wrong legal standard to the facts, in that he “conceived that a principle exists that a brief period of speeding (no matter how excessive the speed) cannot satisfy the mens rea requirement”

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Court of Appeal found trial judge wrongly applied legal standard about brief speeding and mens rea.

propositions.text: Reading reasons as whole, trial judge did not rely on erroneous principle that brief excessive speed alone cannot establish mens rea.
propositions.quote: Reading the reasons as a whole, I am not satisfied that the trial judge relied on the erroneous principle that, as a matter of law, a brief period of excessive speed alone is insufficient to establish the mens rea for dangerous driving.

propositions.text: Momentary excessive speed can establish mens rea if driving is marked departure from reasonable person standard (Roy).
propositions.quote: Momentary excessive speed can establish the mens rea for dangerous driving where, having regard to all the circumstances, the manner of driving supports an inference that the driving was the result of a marked departure from the standard of care that a reasonable person in the same circumstances would have exhibited: R. v. Roy

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge did not rely on erroneous principle; momentary excessive speed can establish mens rea if marked departure.

propositions.text: Trial judge correctly stated legal principles and mens rea test in reasons.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly stated the relevant legal principles applicable to dangerous driving, at paras. 60-66, and restated the mens rea test in the course of his mens rea analysis and conclusion, at paras. 112 and 119.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s case law treatment does not show failure to apply proper principles or constrain assessment by erroneous principle.
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s treatment of case law does not provide a basis to infer that he failed to apply the proper principles or constrained his assessment of all of the circumstances by relying on an erroneous legal principle.

propositions.text: Trial judge engaged in ordinary reasoning by context-based assessment and distinguishing cases.
propositions.quote: The trial judge undertook a context-based assessment of the case law that was presented to him involving excessive speed and made observations about tendencies in that case law. He noted facts that in his view distinguished those cases from the present case. In other words, the trial judge engaged in a completely ordinary method of reasoning.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge correctly stated legal principles and engaged in ordinary reasoning distinguishing cases.

propositions.text: Trial judge was aware that excessive speed and momentary conduct can meet marked departure standard depending on circumstances.
propositions.quote: Read fairly and as a whole, the reasons disclose that the trial judge was aware that both excessive speed and momentary conduct could meet the marked departure standard, depending on the circumstances.

propositions.text: Trial judge cited Doherty J.A. in Willock that conduct in 2-3 seconds can be marked departure.
propositions.quote: he explicitly referred to the statement of Doherty J.A. in R. v. Willock (2006), 212 O.A.C. 82, at para. 31, that “[t]here can be no doubt that conduct occurring in a two to three second interval can amount to a marked departure from the standard of a reasonable person”: para. 117.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge knew excessive speed and momentary conduct can be marked departures and cited Willock.

propositions.text: Trial judge considering momentariness critical does not mean he thought momentary speed cannot satisfy mens rea.
propositions.quote: That the trial judge considered it “critical” that the appellant’s excessive speed was momentary does not mean that he understood that the appellant’s conduct could not, as a matter of law, satisfy the mens rea requirement.

propositions.text: Momentariness was an important factor; trial judge not required to address every factor but explain important ones.
propositions.quote: It suggests that he considered the momentariness of the appellant’s excessive speed to be an important factor in the circumstances. The trial judge was not required to touch on every circumstantial factor in the course of his analysis, but on those he considered important, so as to explain why he reached his conclusion

propositions.text: Questions about weight of factors are not questions of law alone (J.M.H.).
propositions.quote: Questions about whether the trial judge should have placed less weight on the short duration of speeding, and more weight on the degree to which speeding exceeded the limit, where the speeding occurred, or on other factors relating to the appellant’s control of the car and awareness, are not questions of law alone: J.M.H., at para. 28.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge’s focus on momentariness was a factor, not legal error; weighting factors is not a pure legal question.

propositions.text: No basis to infer trial judge failed to compare appellant’s conduct to reasonable person’s in concluding reasonable doubt existed.
propositions.quote: There is also no basis for inferring that the trial judge did not compare the appellant’s conduct to what a reasonable person would have done in the circumstances in coming to the conclusion that there was “at least a reasonable doubt that [the appellant’s] conduct amounted to a marked departure from the standard of a reasonably prudent driver”

propositions.text: Trial judge understood marked departure is a matter of degree and mens rea test is comparative.
propositions.quote: He understood that what represents a marked departure in the circumstances is a matter of degree, and that the mens rea test is fundamentally comparative

propositions.text: Inferring failure to compare because trial judge did not explicitly describe reasonable person’s conduct presumes misunderstanding of law.
propositions.quote: Inferring that the trial judge failed to compare the appellant’s conduct to that of a reasonable person because he did not explicitly describe what a reasonable person would have done in the circumstances is tantamount to presuming that he misunderstood the applicable legal principles.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no basis to infer trial judge failed to compare conduct to reasonable person and understood mens rea test is comparative.

propositions.text: Roy’s two questions assist trial judges but do not change the nature of the mens rea test.
propositions.quote: The two questions this Court identified in Roy, at para. 36, were set out to assist trial judges in determining whether the mens rea test is met in the circumstances. They do not change the nature of the mens rea test.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Roy’s two questions assist trial judges but do not alter the mens rea test’s nature.

propositions.text: The core issue was the second question in Roy about marked departure from standard of care.
propositions.quote: The core issue in this case was the second question in Roy, whether the accused’s failure to foresee the risk and take steps to avoid it was a marked departure from the standard of care expected of a reasonable person in the accused’s circumstances.

propositions.text: The first question in Roy about foreseeability was not the substance of the issue.
propositions.quote: The first question in Roy, whether a reasonable person in the accused’s circumstances would have foreseen the risk and taken steps to avoid it, was not the “substance of what was in issue”: J.M.H., at para. 32, citing Walker, at para. 20.

propositions.text: At trial, appellant appeared to concede the first question affirmatively.
propositions.quote: At trial, the appellant appeared to concede that it could be answered affirmatively: see para. 57.

propositions.text: Trial judge not required to resolve effectively uncontested issues.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was not required to spend his time resolving issues that were effectively uncontested.

propositions.text: Trial judge implicitly answered first question by finding appellant’s failure to foresee risk was a mere departure from normal driving.
propositions.quote: In any event, the trial judge implicitly answered the first question by finding that the appellant’s failure to foresee the risk was aptly described as “a departure or a mere departure from the normal manner of driving”: para. 116, citing R. v. Adams, 2012 PECA 15, 325 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 93, at para. 65.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the core issue is the second Roy question about marked departure; the first question was conceded by appellant and implicitly answered by trial judge.

propositions.text: Trial judge had reasonable doubt whether driving met mens rea standard of marked departure.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was ultimately left with a reasonable doubt as to whether the manner of driving met the mens rea standard, that is, whether it supported an inference that the driving was the result of a marked departure from the standard of care.

propositions.text: Whether trial judge’s acquittal decision was reasonable is not at issue in Crown appeal.
propositions.quote: As stated above, whether his decision to acquit on that basis was “reasonable” under the circumstances is not at issue in a Crown appeal such as this one: J.M.H., at para. 25; Biniaris, at para. 33.

propositions.text: Court finds no legal error in trial judge’s acquittal and would allow appeal to restore acquittal.
propositions.quote: Because I do not find that the trial judge’s decision to acquit is tainted by legal error, I would allow the appeal and restore the acquittal.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed, Karakatsanis J. dissenting.
propositions.quote: Appeal dismissed, Karakatsanis J. dissenting.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondent named.
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellant: Fowler and Blok, Vancouver. Solicitor for the respondent: Attorney General of British Columbia, Vancouver.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge had reasonable doubt on mens rea; court finds no legal error and allows appeal to restore acquittal; appeal dismissed with dissent.
